key_insight: A transferable, physics-based spectral theory predicts which alloying elements compete for or share grain-boundary sites using elemental descriptors rather than alloy-specific atomistic calculations.
engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate grain-boundary chemistry screening for multicomponent alloys, including steels and high-entropy alloys.
method: Represent segregation spectra through local strain and bond deficit, linked to atomic size and surface enthalpy.
Predict cross-species spectral correlations to distinguish site competition from site sharing.
Use a closed-system model incorporating host redistribution, coupled sublattices, compound formation, and solute pairing.
evidence_signal: Calibrated only on binary spectra, the theory achieved unseen-host mean correlation r = 0.81, ranked competition across 870 solute pairs with Spearman ρ = 0.90, and reproduced 11/12 Fe and 49/55 Mg equilibrium ternaries without multicomponent fitting.
watch_item: Metal–metalloid pair chemistry can cause deviations from baseline site competition that still require atomistic resolution.
paper_title: A macroscopic-atom spectral theory of grain-boundary segregation in multicomponent alloys
